newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Beige Book in the limelight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Beige Book in the limelight.

text.p: A bearish U.S. Treasury market will scrutinize the Federal Reserve's Beige Book on Wednesday in an effort to find fresh clues on where the economy is heading, analysts said.
"The Beige Book is going to be examined very carefully for signs that the Fed is finding evidence of more wage pressure and/or price pressures," said Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust.
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release its Beige Book economic survey on Wednesday at 1200 EDT/1600 GMT.
Analysts said they expect the Beige Book show hints of tighter labor markets, signs of accelerating wages and some firming in commodity prices but tame inflation numbers for finished goods.

"We expect to see more of the same, but more of more of the same," Kasriel said, referring to the possibility the Beige Book may confirm a trend but also herald some fresh information on wages and on the labor market.
Also, analysts said final goods demand is expected to be firm in the Beige Book, with consumer spending and the manufacturing sector doing a little better.
"It should be a fairly robust report for the economy as a whole," Kasriel said.

The market is going into the Beige Book with its mood dramatically deteriorated after Federal Reserve Board governor Janet Yellen said in an interview with Reuters on Tuesday the U.S. economy is in an "inflationary danger zone."
Pundits said Yellen's remarks increased the likelihood of a tightening of monetary policy at the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meeting on September 24.
"People are fairly bearish here," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
Analysts said the market's consensus appears to believe the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points at the FOMC meeting on September 24.
But some scattered opinions about a possible 50 basis point rate increase re-emerged on Tuesday after Yellen's comments hit the wires.
"I heard some people talking about 50 basis points again. I guess we'll have to live with that until the end of the month now," said a trader at a U.S. primatry dealership.
Also, analysts said the market sees the possible September rate hike as the first of a series.
"What's ... keeping the bond market from rallying back is that history tells you there are never any limited one-shot tightening moves," Kasriel said.
"We could be getting ready to see a string of moves. That's why bonds are as weak as they are," he added.
Analysts said, however, the market is still expected to remain rangebound, with the current range for the benchmark 30-year bond yield seen between 7.00 and 7.25 percent.
"If we enter the Beige Book ... above 7-1/8 percent in terms of bond yield we're not going to back up a terribly large amount," Rupkey said.
The 6-3/4 percent bellwether bond was quoted down 20/32 at 95-12/32 in late Tuesday trading to yield 7.13 percent.
On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve injected reserves in the banking system via two-day system repurchase agreements, when the federal funds rate was trading at 5-3/16 percent.
The funds rate is seen opening at 5.31 percent on Wednesday, above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target.
